title: Java in practice
lead: This project is first of all a Java demo, and this page shows the Java techniques behind its speed: plain numeric code, the Vector API, GPU kernels with TornadoVM and more. Each comes with an excerpt of the real code and a measured speed-up, compared with C++ where measured. It ends with Java and React without a REST layer.
toc.outlook: Outlook: Valhalla and the final Vector API
sec.overview.title: Java in this project
sec.overview.p1: Five Java techniques in this project have a measured effect. Plain Java without an object per move runs the classical search at about {n:1.6} million nodes per second on one core. The {term:vector-api|Vector API} makes the {term:forward-pass|forward pass} of the network about 15 times faster than scalar Java. {term:tornadovm|TornadoVM} moves it to the GPU. {term:virtual-thread|Virtual threads} feed that GPU during training, and {term:teavm|TeaVM} brings the Java search into the browser.
sec.overview.p2: The figure puts the forward pass of the {term:small-large|SMALL} network on one log axis. As a rough rule from these measurements: incremental updates in plain Java gave tens of percent, SIMD a factor of about 15, and a GPU with large batches another factor of about 37. At batch 1 the GPU loses. Only the three Mac rows come from one run; the others come from other machines and runs, so read them as orders of magnitude, not as exact ratios.
sec.overview.p3: A note on measuring Java: the {term:jit|JIT compiler} turns hot bytecode into machine code only while the program runs, so the first calls are slower. Every benchmark here therefore starts with an untimed warm-up round. The JIT even shows in results: the Vector API network gave last-digit differences between its first and later calls on the same input, probably interpreted code against compiled code.
sec.plain-java.title: Fast plain Java
sec.plain-java.p1: Java gets fast when the hot path allocates nothing. A move is an `int`, `from | (to << 8)`, not an object. The board is a `byte[]` with the owner of each cell, plus a piece list per player. The search plays and takes back moves on one mutable position ({term:make-unmake|make/unmake}) and keeps the undo data in parallel primitive arrays. Move generation fills a buffer of the caller. The jump search keeps its visited set of {n:121} cells in two `long` values, so it stays in registers ({src:engine/src/main/java/sternhalma/engine/Position.java}).
sec.plain-java.p2: The same idea helped the evaluation. About two thirds of a leaf evaluation went into one {term:feature}, the best one-move gain. An incremental version updates its sums in make and unmake instead of recomputing them ({src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/IncrementalLinear.java}). With identical search trees, the search became about {n:1.3} times faster in nodes per second, and self-play played about {n:1.45} times as many games per CPU second. The machine was busy with other jobs during these runs, so the numbers are indicative.
sec.plain-java.p3: A faithful C++ port, with the same algorithms and move order and no extra optimisation, runs the same search {n:1.5} to {n:1.7} times as fast: about {n:2.6} against {n:1.6} million nodes per CPU second on one core of an Apple M3 Max, in one native run. That C++ build keeps {term:bounds-check|bounds checks} on, as Java always does; they cost C++ 11 to 13 %. The JVM also starts slower: about {n:0.85} s against {n:0.26} s to the end of a one-position search ({term:cold-start|cold start}).
sec.vector-api.title: SIMD with the Vector API
sec.vector-api.p1: {term:simd|SIMD} means that one CPU instruction works on several numbers at once: 4 floats with NEON on the Mac, 8 with AVX2 and 16 with AVX-512 on Intel. The {term:vector-api|Vector API} gives plain Java access to these instructions. A {term:vector-species|species} fixes the vector width. The project picks it once in a `static final` field, because the JIT compiles vector code only for a constant species. The inner loop of the convolution loads 2 weight vectors, broadcasts 4 input cells and runs 8 {term:fma|fused multiply-adds} into 8 accumulators.
sec.vector-api.p2: On one M3 Max core this is about 15 times faster than the scalar Java reference. One Intel Sapphire Rapids core with AVX-512 is about 3 times faster than the same core with AVX2. Against hand-written C++ SIMD on the Mac, C++ is about 12 % ahead for the {term:small-large|LARGE} network at batch 256. Without FMA in C++ both are equal; the Java Vector API always uses FMA. A tile with 16 accumulators was 4 times slower, probably because HotSpot did not keep 16 vectors in registers.
sec.vector-api.p3: The API is still an {term:incubator-module|incubator module}: the build adds `--add-modules jdk.incubator.vector`, and the JVM prints a warning at start. Without the module, the code falls back to the scalar network ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/Networks.java}). One story from the cloud: in the first run on an AVX-512 machine, C++ was about 5 times slower than Java. The cause was a defect of the C++ port, with bounds checks and a stack copy in the inner loop. After the fix, C++ was about {n:1.3} times faster; the source rates that figure as indicative.
sec.auto-vectorization.title: Auto-vectorization: not used here
sec.auto-vectorization.p1: With {term:auto-vectorization|auto-vectorization}, the compiler turns an ordinary loop into SIMD instructions by itself. HotSpot's C2 compiler can do this for simple counted loops over primitive arrays. That is textbook background: this project does not rely on it and never measured it. No benchmark compares a loop vectorized by the JIT with the Vector API, and no build file sets a related JVM flag. Whether C2 vectorizes any loop of this project was not checked.
sec.auto-vectorization.p2: The project writes its vector code by hand instead. The JIT recognises only some loop shapes, and it does not reorder floating-point sums, because a different order changes the result. So nobody can rely on it for a loop like the hex convolution. The scalar reference even sums in `double` in a fixed order on purpose: it is the oracle that the fast versions are tested against ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/ReferenceOps.java}). On the C++ side, GCC's auto-vectorizer does not touch the corresponding loop either; that loop is vectorized by hand.
sec.tornadovm.title: GPU kernels with TornadoVM
sec.tornadovm.p1: A GPU runs thousands of small threads at once. A {term:kernel} is the function that each of them runs for one work item. {term:tornadovm|TornadoVM} compiles Java methods into such kernels at run time, for Metal on the Mac and CUDA on Linux. The two outer loops of the convolution carry `@Parallel`, and TornadoVM turns them into the GPU grid, one work item per output value. A {term:task-graph|task graph} says what to copy and what to run: the weights go to the GPU once, the inputs on every call.
sec.tornadovm.p2: At batch 256 the GPU of the M3 Max computes about {n:110000} evaluations per second for the SMALL network, about 37 times one Vector API thread. At batch 1 the GPU loses: a warm call has a fixed cost of {n:0.3} to {n:0.5} ms, and one CPU thread is {n:1.5} times faster. On an NVIDIA Tesla T4, TornadoVM and hand-written CUDA reach the same throughput, about {n:85000} evaluations per second. One Java source serves Metal and CUDA: {n:1372} non-comment lines of code against {n:1714} for the two C++ backends.
sec.tornadovm.p3: A new TornadoVM process on the T4 needs 3 to {n:4.4} s to its first result, C++ CUDA about {n:0.2} s. The batch size is compiled into the kernel, so the project rounds batches up to a power of two, one {term:bucket} per compiled plan, and a {term:kernel-choice-rule|kernel-choice rule} picks the kernel per bucket. A kernel has no {term:bounds-check|bounds checks}: a read past the end returns 0. Metal's `tanh` returns 0 or NaN for large arguments. Unsupported Java fails with an `Error`, not an exception.
sec.outlook.title: Outlook: Valhalla and the final Vector API
sec.outlook.p1: Two OpenJDK developments would change this code. The Vector API is in its twelfth incubation, JEP 537, delivered in JDK 27. The JEP says it will incubate until the necessary features of Project Valhalla become available as preview features. JEP 401, value objects, is targeted to JDK 28 as a preview; JDK 28 is scheduled for general availability in March 2027. As of 21 November 2026, no Vector API JEP is listed for JDK 28. The project compiles with `--release 25` and uses none of this.
sec.outlook.p2: Instances of a {term:value-class|value class} are immutable and have no identity. In exchange, a JVM can store them flat in arrays and fields instead of as separate objects on the heap. The example in JEP 401 is the declaration `value record Point(int x, int y)`. JEP 537 expects the vector classes, such as `FloatVector`, to become value classes.
sec.outlook.p3: The block below is an illustration, not code of this project; it was neither compiled nor measured. It writes `Move` as a value record instead of a packed `int`. The vector loop would look almost the same; the incubator flag and its warning would go away. Whether a JVM would really flatten `Move[]`, and how fast that would be, is open: JEP 401 says that a JVM can do it, not that it will.
sec.more.title: Also in the code
sec.more.p1: {term:virtual-thread|Virtual threads} feed the GPU during self-play. Each game runs as a virtual thread, and one {term:device-thread|device thread} collects their positions and calls the GPU. A first version used a semaphore over 256 platform threads and reached {n:29000} to {n:46000} evaluations per second, against {n:57000} to {n:82000} with virtual threads, measured minutes apart: roughly {n:1.8} times. On a T4, 512 games on 4 {term:carrier-thread|carrier threads} kept the device thread busy 99 % of the time. One pitfall: a virtual thread has no CPU time of its own.
sec.more.p2: {term:teavm|TeaVM} compiles the Java search to {term:wasm-gc|WebAssembly GC}, and that build is the default engine of this site. In Node.js on the M3 Max it reaches about {n:0.96} million nodes per second, about {n:0.7} times the JVM and about half of the C++ WebAssembly build. The Wasm file has about 610 kB, 210 kB with gzip. The forward pass stays in C++: scalar Java compiled by TeaVM reached only 126 to 163 positions per second, C++ WebAssembly about {n:3100}. The browser has no Vector API.
sec.more.p3: The {term:ffm-api|Foreign Function & Memory API} works behind TornadoVM. Its arrays are off-heap memory segments, and the project copies into them with `MemorySegment.copy` ({src:nn-tornado/src/main/java/sternhalma/tornado/OpsCopy.java}). TornadoVM's CUDA backend calls the driver through `java.lang.foreign`; the project calls no native code of its own. Checked and not in use: GraalVM native image and Gradle toolchains. `Long.expand` and `Long.compress` are an open question, not measured yet.
sec.hilla.title: Java and React without REST
sec.hilla.p1: The online mode runs the engines on a Spring Boot server, and no hand-written REST layer sits between the React page and the server. One Java class carries `@BrowserCallable`, which makes it a {term:browser-callable|browser-callable service}. During the build, {term:hilla|Hilla} generates a TypeScript client for its public methods. The method `choose` returns the Java record `ServerChoice`, and Hilla generates a TypeScript interface with the same fields. The class is a normal Spring bean with constructor injection ({src:app/src/main/java/sternhalma/app/GameEndpoint.java}).
sec.hilla.p2: The React code loads the generated client with a dynamic import and passes it on as a small interface, so the adapter knows nothing about Hilla and its tests run without it ({src:web/src/engines/server/load.ts}). In the offline build, Vite drops the import, and the build script checks that no file contains `connect/`. On the wire, each method is a `POST /connect/GameEndpoint/<method>` with the parameters as a JSON object; the answer is the record as JSON. The page adds a {term:csrf-token|CSRF token} in a header by itself.
sec.hilla.p3: The limits, as the code shows them: the server engines play only the default variant and have no analysis. The endpoint allows anonymous calls, and the app binds to `127.0.0.1` by default. The jar copies the engine and table files of the web app but not the network models ({src:app/build.gradle.kts}), so the net engines in the browser probably lack their models in the online build; this comes from reading the build script and was not tried. CI does not run the Hilla production build.

fig.javaspeed.desc: A dot chart on a logarithmic axis, in evaluations per second of the SMALL network. The first group has three rows from one run on an Apple M3 Max: scalar Java at batch 1, the Vector API on one thread and TornadoVM on the GPU, both at batch 256. The second group has rows from other machines: the Vector API with AVX-512, TornadoVM and C++ CUDA on a Tesla T4, and scalar Java via TeaVM and C++ WebAssembly in the browser.
